It was a case that shook a small New Jersey suburb to its core.

On August 7th, 1972, sixteen-year-old Jeannette DePalma walked out of her home in the sleepy township of Springfield, and into the realm of urban legend. She had planned to hitchhike to a friend’s house before an afternoon shift at work. She would never make it.

Six weeks after seemingly vanishing into thin air, the body of Jeannette DePalma was found after a local dog brought the teenager’s decomposed arm back to its owner. A search party discovered the rest of her remains high atop of a cliff inside an abandoned quarry. For decades, this eerie outcropping of roch had been known to locals as the Devil’s Teeth.

The local police tried to diffuse this situation by quietly suggesting to others that girl must have been partying with friends in the woods, and overdosed. The fact that Jeannette’s body was so badly decomposed made the determination of a cause of death uncertain. According to the first-responders who climbed the Devil’s Teeth, Jeannette body was found surrounded by occult objects, suggesting that a ritual sacrifice had taken place.

Rumors of witchcraft and Satanism were splashed across the headlines of every local paper in the county. News of Jeannette’s supposed Satanic murder traveled as far as Iowa. The terrified citizens of Springfield began to demand answers. How could something like this happen in such a nice, middle-class community? The DePalma family suggested to reporters that Jeannette could have been targeted by Satanists or modern-day witches due to her activity within her church. However, Jeannette’s parish of choice - an Evangelical center located in the urban city of Elizabeth – quickly distanced themselves from the dead teenager; denying any significant involvement in her life.

While the police and the public were becoming mired in these bizarre subplots, connections to other events in the area were going overlooked – including the deaths of several other young women nearby.

As time passed, the DePalma case vanished from the headlines, and the terrified residents of Springfield seemed more than happy to forget the event, despite the fact that no arrests were ever made.

I'm sick of medics. I'm sick of medics, again. I'm sick of them doing this shit constantly:

  1. They heal randomly and inconsistently. Just for a couple seconds, then they flee. Hey, I'm a heavy, you probably shouldn't get the fuck away from my side to heal some fucking sniper who is perfectly healthy and not even getting shot at.
  2. They stop healing right before moving to the next point or they don't heal right before attacking it. Say I'm about to attack the next point, why are you running towards the point too, not healing a teammate?
  3. They stop healing right before entering combat, defending a point or not. They abandon you, completely, to your luck
  4. They fight against pyros and other lethal classes with the syringe gun. No fucking comments

Okay. OKAY, that's not too bad, is it? It's not BAD to get abandoned by a medic who is running to heal a higher priority class like a Heavy or a Soldier, or someone who is getting hurt. But what if I'm the Heavy or the Soldier and what if I'm getting hurt? What if I get healed for three seconds and then I see the medic flee or I realize the medic isn't healing me when I'm fighting another player? I'd understand that no medic attaches himself to a bad player, but what happens when I'm among the top five players and the medic is among the five worst players of the match (which happens too often)?

Why don't people play medic well? It's not difficult, you just have to keep your team healthy and Über damage dealing classes when necessary. I'm sick of medics, most of them don't understand that their job is to heal, to support the team, not to get kills.

Edit: Typo.

Medics in pubs?

What kind of paradise is this?

This goes two ways. So many people don't protect their medic buddy, or overextend like their pocket medic makes them unstoppable. A medic isn't going to join you to headbutt a wall of rockets and sentries with 80% uber charged when they can hide around the corner and switch to a less foolhardy fellow.
That being said, bad medics are second only to bad engineers in self sabotage. Put away your blutsager, build a teleporter, and don't switch to spy or sniper, we already have three of each.
Exactly this! If I play Soldier, and I overextend for some reason, I always hope that the medic who's pocketing me gets the fuck outta there if his charge isn't ready, because I'd do that as a medic.

1- Just because you're a Heavy doesn't mean you always need a pocket medic, you just got a buff and have the highest health and theoretical DPS in the game anyway. The medic's supposed to spread out the heals to the rest of the team so hopefully everyone nearby's overhealed, until a push is going on and not just the heavy which is the case in most pubs.

2- There's a good chance this could be because you aren't communicating with your medic that you're about to do a push, and they're escaping because you're overextending

3- To be fair, the syringe gun's theoretical max damage is higher tan the flamethrower's theoretical max damage.

Okay, as someone who has put in 80 hours as a medic, I can address situations in which each point raised is a valid and good strategy for a medic.

 

They heal randomly and inconsistently.

I heal 'randomly and inconsistently' when there's a shit ton of people on the battlefield who all need healing and my primary target (usually a heavy) is near full-health or higher. I am not going to let everyone around me die and leave me and one heavy on the battlefield when there's no overall coordinating strategy cause we're just pubbing. We only have numbers, and I will be trying to keep as many teammates up as possible (there are diminishing returns beyond trying to keep 3 people healed at once so it's rarely more than that I focus on). This has the added benefit of raising my uber faster, and most times it is the uber that breaks the choke. If I just keep healing one target that's beyond overhealed, I'm just lagging my uber charging and letting people die. I can't play that way. To be fair to your point though, the heavy remains my primary concern, and he will get the heals when he needs them unless he's acting like a low-grade moron, in which case I will let him die.

 

They stop healing right before moving to the next point or they don't heal right before attacking it.

why are you running towards the point too, not healing a teammate?

I agree that the medic should be healing when moving between points, but I don't understand the question. I attack points as a medic. I do what so many fail to do which is get on the point. I watch so many timid players just sit back even when the enemy has no way of keeping them off the point. Uhhhhh get on the point! If I can keep you healed, take flak on the point and I'll heal you. If you stand off the point, then fine, I'll lead by example and go stand on it and wait for things to click in your brain since by then I've communicated that fact at least once to the team. This is something I just can't understand. Why are people so afraid to stand on an unoccupied point? Force them to push you off it. That's how it works!

 

They stop healing right before entering combat, defending a point or not. They abandon you, completely, to your luck

Not sure how this is happening, but there have been times where I know I'm not leaving my current area because the choke-point is around the corner, and I need to charge an uber. I'll heal people as they go by, but I'm gonna follow fools to my untimely death because they want to run into a meat grinder before I'm charged. One heal from a medic is no commitment; they are not automatically your pocket healer. If you want some kind of strategy where you two roll out together, you better communicate that with them before just strolling into enemy fire. I see people all the time run into dumb shit, I try to heal them as much as I can, but I'm not gonna go run into sentry fire to keep a fool alive when I don't even have an uber charged up (something they can see on their screen when I'm healing them). Also, because there's no strategy, you have no idea which way a medic is gonna run if you're traveling as big pack and reach some fork in the road where you can take different paths to your objective. Medics usually run behind those their healing, and if you go right and the rest of the team goes left, well the medic is probably gonna go with the pack of teammates rather then the one guy who thinks he knows better (especially if the medic has any reason to doubt him). Again, a lack of communication is why this problem and many like it persist. If people actually spoke and said "we should go left because they have a sentry on the right", then maybe everyone would go together and no one would get mad when the medic has chosen to go somewhere else.

 

They fight against pyros and other lethal classes with the syringe gun. No fucking comments

If a medic is doing this over healing more capable teammates, then they are bad medics. But using the syringe gun is a very valid tactic beyond solo situations. If I'm in a fairly open area and healing a so-so grenading demoman and we're fighting against a decent scout, the first thing the scout is going to do is switch targeting to me. Okay, now what good does it do for me to heal the demoman? He's going to have a hell of a time touching the scout who's going to be trying to kill me. And guess what? No ones around to heal me! This is when I pull out my syringe. I already hear you saying, "But oooooo, the scout isn't lethal!" 1. To medics they easily can be. 2. The same situation applies if it's a pyro that we see coming from a distance. He's gonna blow the demomans grenades all around, so the demoman is just handing the pyro his ammo on a platter which is going to be bounced back towards the demoman and myself if I decide to attach myself to the demoman. Instead, I just pull out the syringe and now the pyro is in a 2v1 situation. That's far better than me just healing a foolish demoman wasting his grenades on a pyro. It forces the pyro to come at you. Then you kite away syringing his face. I take down butloads of overconfident pyros in this way. But put me in a small room with one and I'll scream like a schoolgirl and run away. You gotta pick your battles and the insinuation that medics should heal over killing is pretty insulting.

I think comparable complaints to those lodged here can really be applied to any class because bad players play all classes. It just so happens you notice how bad the medics are. Try playing as a medic, you realize how bad all the other classes are being played because you have to interact with all of your teammates. As a soldier, I don't have to worry about what that heavy is doing or why that demoman is going out into sentry fire. But as a medic, those things make up the bulk of your day.

I understand your frustrations in pub games with medics, there are a lot of bad ones, but I think your criticisms are a little too general because there are very valid tactical use cases within all of them and the issues you're seeing actually apply in some form or another to all classes. The failing of a medic is very noticeable to you because you're directly depending on them, but you directly depend on the rest of your team, regardless of the class, to achieve victory.

If you want something actionable, then talk to your team about strategy when pubbing. Wait, stop laughing. Seriously. Not even everyone, just address someone who's playing a medic and tell them your strategy. I'd love it if someone would do that when I'm playing medic. Just say "Look, I'm a heavy and you're a medic and we were made for each other. So let's charge that uber up and push through their sewers."

Instead, as a medic, I get people who'll go out, take some fire, and run back inside without even killing anyone. Over and over. They'll run into sentries. They'll engage in bad matchups. They'll run into packs of enemies that far outgun us. And on and on and on.

TLDR; The knife cuts both ways. Bad players are abound in all multiplayer games. Communication is the key to victory. (Disclaimer: Don't try to generate strategy on a 24/7 2fort or turbine server. No one plays on those to win; they just like to kill.)
